mechaber.en:
How four cubits are allotted for a house or courtyard, the manure of a courtyard, and billeting. This siman contains nine seifim.
When a courtyard is divided, four cubits are allotted to each doorway and the remainder is divided equally, because every doorway requires four cubits extending into the courtyard. Even if the doorway is very wide, the owner receives four cubits extending into the courtyard across its entire width. If the doorway is less than four cubits wide, its allotment is widened on the sides so that he receives an area of four by four cubits. If one house opening into the courtyard has two doorways and another has only one, the owner of the first receives four cubits for each doorway according to its width, while the owner of the single doorway receives only four cubits in front of it. This applies where two persons acquired ownerless land, such as where one built a house with two doorways and the other built a house with one doorway, and afterward they enclosed the area to form a courtyard. Rama: Some say the same applies if a father orally divided his property and gave one son a house with two doorways and another a house with one doorway. If, however, two persons jointly purchased or inherited the property, they acquired or inherited equal shares in both the houses and the courtyard, and neither receives more than the other. Even if they first divided the houses before dividing the courtyard, the person who received the house with two doorways does not thereby acquire four cubits in the courtyard for each doorway. Rather, the courtyard is divided equally.

Who acquired. The Sema writes that they distinguished between the cases in order to resolve the rule that brothers who divided an inheritance have no right of way, window, ladder, or water channel against one another. They therefore explain that there the brothers inherited their father's property, whereas here they acquired ownerless property. From the Tur it appears that Rashi distinguished differently: here the father divided his property between his two sons by his own directive, as the Rama states, unlike an ordinary inheritance. The Rosh explains that the case of the brothers concerns a division made by appraisal, where one brother paid the other an equalizing payment. These explanations need not disagree, for each authority stated one applicable circumstance. The Shach writes that it appears to him that the text should read, "not by appraisal and without an equalizing payment"; examine this carefully. See also siman 173, seif 3, and the Rosh. It is nevertheless possible, albeit with difficulty, to retain the text without emendation: the case of the brothers concerns one who made an equalizing payment, yet they still do not obtain against one another window rights to the extent required for four cubits, or alternatively he has windows from another place; see there. With respect to the four cubits required for entrances and for a vineyard, however, a greater right is needed, and therefore one who made an equalizing payment does acquire it. So writes the Shach. (See also what the Taz writes on this matter.)

kessef_hakodashim.en: Four cubits; see Sema, seif katan 2. Concerning the four cubits assigned to an entrance in siman 172, as discussed by the Tur there and in the glosses from the Perishah printed in the newer editions of the Tur, I am uncertain whether the four cubits of courtyard space, in addition to the four cubits belonging to the doorway itself, are assigned only on the side where the doorway opens, or along every side of the walls within the courtyard. The implication of the Tur, those glosses, and the Sema at the beginning of the siman is that even for the courtyard space one receives only an area of four cubits by four cubits, no more, so that together with the four cubits belonging to the doorway there are four by eight cubits, as stated in the glosses. One might have thought that at least the entire width of the wall containing the doorway receives a depth of four cubits, and that even where the wall itself is narrower than four cubits he nevertheless receives four by four cubits, just as a doorway narrower than four cubits still receives four cubits. The sources, however, do not read that way. He receives only four by eight cubits in front of the doorway, and any additional area is divided equally. The four by eight cubits must be rectangular, as stated by the Tur. This must be reconciled with the Rosh regarding mezuzah, where a true four by four cubit square is required, whereas Rambam holds that it is sufficient if the area is capable of being squared, as in Yoreh Deah 286:13 and the Shach there. Here it appears that Rambam does not dispute the Rif and Rosh that an actual rectangular area is required, although the Gemara in Sukkah 3a appears to compare the cases. This requires study. As to shop structures adjoining an entrance, what are called a ledge or stall, whether they count as part of the doorway for purposes of the four cubits, it appears that only an opening that reaches to ground level lies within the four cubits.

Which they acquired or inherited. This distinction reconciles the rule that brothers who divided have no right of way against one another. Some explain that the rule there concerns inherited property, while here it concerns property acquired from ownerless status. The dissent cited by Rama explains that there it concerns a grantor who divided his property. The Rosh explains that the rule concerning brothers refers to division without valuation and equalization, while the present rule refers to division with valuation. rabbi_akiva_eiger.he: [שו"ע] אלא חולקים בשוה. נ"ב אם החצר ה' על ה' א"י בעל ב' פתחים לומר כיון דיגיע לחלקו רק ד"א לפ"א וד"א בחצר אין בזה דין חלוקה ולא אחלוק עד שיהי' בחצר ו' פעמים ד' על ד' כדי שיגיע לו ג' פעמים ד' על ד' דכל שיגיע לו ד"א לפתח אחד וד"א בחצר מקרי יש בו דין חלוקה. הרא"ש ז"ל:
rabbi_akiva_eiger.en: [Shulchan Aruch] Rather, they divide equally. Note: If a courtyard is five cubits by five cubits, the owner of two doorways cannot say, "Since my share will leave only four cubits for one doorway and four cubits in the courtyard, the property is not divisible, and I will not divide unless the courtyard is six times four by four so that I receive three areas of four by four." Whenever he receives four cubits for one doorway and four cubits in the courtyard, it is considered legally divisible. So rules the Rosh.

siftei_kohen.he:
חצר המתחלקת כו' עיין בתשו' ן' לב כלל ט"ו סי' פ"ח:
ויש אומרים דה"ה אם חלק נכסיו על פיו כו' והב"ח הוכיח דגם ר"י הלוי מודה בזה והאריך להוכיח כן מסוגיא פ"ק דסוכה ע"ש:
אבל שנים שקנו או שירשו כו' עיין בסמ"ע ס"ק ד' עד והרא"ש מוקי לה דההוא דאחין כו' מיירי דחלקו בשומא והעלה אחד לחבירו כו' ונ"ל להגיה שלא בשומ' ולא העלה נ"ל ודוק וע"ל סי' קע"ג ס"ג ועיין בהרא"ש ויש לדחוק בלא שום הג"ה דה"ק דההיא דאחי' כו' מיירי בהעל' ומ"מ אין להם חלונות זע"ז [כי א"צ] כ"כ חלונות כמו שצריך לד"א א"צ שיש לו חלונו' ממקום אחר ע"ש אבל בר"ה של פתחים ושל כרם צריך יותר ולכך בהעלה יש לו ודוק:
siftei_kohen.en:
A courtyard that can be divided, etc. See Responsa Mahari ibn Lev, rule 15, siman 88.
"And there is a saying that if some of his assets are under his mouth, and the U.S. has demonstrated a R&D model, he is grateful to this and he will continue to prove that he is a member of the United States."
"But the years that we have made, or shall be seen," he said, "and shall not be seen in the heavens, and shall be given to them."

turei_zahav.he: [ס"א בד"א בשנים שקנו מן ההפקר כו']. בב"י כתב לכאורה נראה דר"י הלוי לא פי' כן אלא אפלוגתא דרב הונא ור"ח כו' ואח"כ כתב אבל מדברי הרמב"ם כו' ואפשר כו' כל זה תמוה מאוד דברור הוא דרבי יוחנן ס"ל ממש כר"ח ור"י מיירי בין בהפקר בין בירושה דקנייה כל חד בדינא דהיינו שאין א' כופה את חבירו לחלוק אא"כ יש לו בהפקר ד"א לכל פתח מה שזכה מצד פתחים וכפי מ"ש רבינו ס"ס זה ואם הוא בירושה וקנייה צריך שיהיה עכ"פ ד"א לפתח א' וכן בהפקר בפתחיהן שוות ואע"פ שגם חבירו יקח מ"מ הוא מעכב החלוקה עד שיהיו לשניהם כך וב"י העתיק בסמוך סיום דברי הר"י מגא"ש ולפניו אויר שיש בו ד' על ד' הוא ט"ס וצ"ל ד' על ח' וכן הוא בהדיא במ"מ ואין כאן שום חילוק דעת בין הרמב"ם לשאר פוסקים דלכ"ע מתפרשין דברי ר' יוחנן בין בהפקר בין בירושה וקנייה כמ"ש וגם הקושיא שמקשה ב"י אינה קשה כלל לפי מ"ש דר' יוחנן לא נחית כלל לפרש דין פתחים מה שיש להם דבא לומר דכל א' מעכב החלוקה עד שיהיה לכל פתח ד"א דהיינו כ"א כדינו בעלמא:
turei_zahav.en: Seif 1: When does this apply? When two persons acquired from ownerless property. The Beit Yosef writes that at first glance Rabbi Yosef Halevi explained the dispute of Rav Huna and Rav Chisda only in one context, and later suggests that the Rambam differs. This is very surprising. It is clear that Rabbi Yochanan follows Rav Chisda, and that Rabbi Yosef Halevi speaks both of ownerless property and of inheritance. Each party acquires according to the governing law. Thus, one cannot compel his fellow to divide unless, in a case of ownerless property, each entrance receives four cubits based on what was acquired through the entrances, as Rabbeinu writes at the end of this siman. In inheritance or purchase, there must at least be four cubits for one entrance. The same applies in ownerless property where the entrances are equal. Even though his fellow will also receive an allotment, one may withhold division until each receives the proper amount. The Beit Yosef later quotes the end of Rabbi Yosef Halevi's words as saying that there must be open space of four by four before the entrance. This is a scribal error. It should read four by eight, as the Maggid Mishneh states explicitly. There is no disagreement between the Rambam and the other authorities. All agree that Rabbi Yochanan's ruling applies both to ownerless property and to inheritance or purchase. The Beit Yosef's question is also no question, for Rabbi Yochanan did not seek to define the rights attached to the entrances. He merely taught that each owner may withhold division until every entrance receives four cubits, each according to the law applicable to him.

mechaber.he: בד"א כששני הבתים שוים וחלקו בית כנגד בית ולא הוצרכו לשום אותם ולהעלות בדמים אבל אם אינם שוים ושמו אותם והעלום בדמים ואותו שהגיע לחלקו הבית שיש בו שני פתחים נתן לחבירו הדמים ששוה יותר על שלו בכלל זה העילוי ג"כ ד' אמות שבחצר וזכה בהם כמו שזכה במה שביתו שוה יותר משל האחר אע"פ שבעוד שלא חלקו לא היו הד' אמות שלו לגמרי אלא לפרק בו משאו וחבירו היה משתמש בו ג"כ כשהיה מוצא אותם פנויים עתה שחלקו הם שלו לגמרי: הגה וכל זה מיירי בסתם חצירות אבל חצר שיש לכל אחד חלק ידוע כל אחד אינו נוטל אלא כפי מה שיש לו ואם מגיע לכל אחד לפני ביתו ד' אמות על ד' אמות חולקין בין אם יש לבית פתחים הרבה או לא (טור):
mechaber.en:
At the same time, the two houses were housed against a house, and were not consumed by any of them, but if they were not put in their mouths and put them in the hands of the blood and the one who came to the part of the house in which two of them had been given to the blood that was not entirely known to him, but that he was not known as any of the other
Everyone comes before his house, D.Y., divided whether there is a lot of openings or not

beer_hagolah.he:
ז) שם ס"ד בשם אביו הרא"ש:
ח) לאו דוקא דה"ה אם נתן בעל פתח הא' לבעל שני הפתחים דמים דכיון דאיכ' שומא ועילוי איכא למימר דשמו גם כן עילוי ארבע אמות שבחצר ואם שמו שיתן בעל פתח האחד לחבירו עשרה זהובים י"ל שאלו לא היה לו אלא פתח אחד ג"כ היו שמים שיתן לו עשרים כן דקדק הב"י מדברי הרא"ש וכיוצא מזה כ' ה"ה בפ"ב מהל' שכנים דין א' בשם הרשב"א ושכן נ"ל מדברי רבינו חננאל:
beer_hagolah.en:
The name of his father is the name of his father:
This is not literal. The same applies if the owner of one entrance paid money to the owner of two entrances. Since there was an appraisal and adjustment, we may say they also appraised the advantage of the four cubits in the courtyard. If they appraised that the owner of one entrance should pay his fellow ten gold coins, perhaps if he too had only one entrance they would have appraised twenty. Beit Yosef infers this from Rosh. The Maggid Mishneh writes similarly in Hilkhot Shekhenim chapter 2, law 1, in the name of Rashba and says it also appears from Rabbenu Chananel.

beur_hagra.he:
בד"א כו'. מהנ"ל ב' אחין ועלו להדדי:
אע"פ שבעוד. כמ"ש בתוספתא וירושלמי הביאם הרא"ש שם:
עתה. כיון דעלו להדדי וע"ש:
וכ"ז מיירי כו' אבל. ר"ל בכה"ג שאמר בס"א אבל שנים שקנו או כו' דא"צ אלא ד"א לכ"א חוץ מהראוי לפתח א' כגון שני אחים צריך בחצר שמנה על שמנה ועברי"מ וברא"ש:
beur_hagra.en:
When does this apply... From the case above of two brothers who raised the value against one another.
Even though while... As stated in the Tosefta and Yerushalmi cited there by the Rosh.
Now. Since they raised the value against one another; see there.
All this concerns... but. Meaning, a case such as that stated in seif 1. But two who purchased, or the like, require only four amos for each, in addition to the area appropriate for one entrance. Thus, for example, two brothers require a courtyard of eight by eight amos. See the Yad Ramah and the Rosh.

meirat_einayim.he:
כששני הבתים שווים כו' ה"ה כשאינם שווים ולא חלקוהו בשומא ועילוי אלא אורחא דמילתא כ' הטור והמחבר ועפ"ר:
ואותו שהגיע לחלקו הבית שיש בו שני פתחים נתן כו' ה"ה אם הבית שיש בו פתח א' עדיף מהבית שיש בו שני פתחי' והוא נתן לבית של ב' פתחים העודף זכה ג"כ בעל ב' פתחים לכל פתח ד"א דאמרי' דאלולי זה הי' צריך ליתן לו עודף יותר ובפרישה כתבתי די"ל דלרבות' נקט הטור והמחבר דאותו שיש לו שני פתחים נותן העודף דה"א כיון דהעלה סתם ולא הזכיר שבשביל הב' פחחים מעלה לו לא היה דעתו עליהן קמ"ל וכ"ש אם בעל פתח א' העל' לבעל ב' פתחים דשם אין ריעותא כלל במה דלא הזכיר בעלוייו שיש לה שני פתחים דמה לו להזכיר טובתו של השני וק"ל:
בכלל זה העילוי כו' פי' אע"ג דעלו סתם ולא הזכירו הד"א:
meirat_einayim.en:
When the two houses are equal, etc. The same law applies even when they are unequal and the parties did not divide them by appraisal and monetary equalization. The Tur and Mechaber merely stated the usual case. See the Perishah.
The one whose lot was the house with two entrances paid, etc. The same applies if the house with one entrance is superior to the house with two entrances and its owner paid the one receiving the two-entrance house the excess value. The owner of the two-entrance house still receives four amot for each entrance, because otherwise the payment would have needed to be larger. In the Perishah I wrote that perhaps the Tur and Mechaber state specifically the case where the owner of the two-entrance house pays the excess as the greater novelty. One might have thought that because the extra payment was made generally, without saying it was on account of the second entrance, the additional four amot were not included. The ruling teaches otherwise. All the more so where the one-entrance owner pays the two-entrance owner, because there is then no weakness in failing to mention that the other house has two entrances. Why would he need to mention the other's advantage?
This enhancement is included, etc. Meaning, even though they made the valuation generally and did not expressly mention the four amot.

netivot_hamishpat_beurim.he: אבל חצר שיש לכ"א חלק ידוע הרבה תמוה לי הגה"ה זאת דאם כוונתו שכ"א מכיר חלקו ואין א' משתמש בשל חבירו א"כ אפי' אין מגיע לכל בית רק פחות מד"א חולקין כמבואר לעיל בסי' קע"א סעיף ב' ואם כוונתו שיש לכ"א חלק ידוע היינו שקנאו או שירשו שידוע שכ"א יש לו החצי או שא' בכור וחלקו ידוע שהוא פי שנים או שקנה שני חלקים ומ"ש בסתם חצירות כוונתו שקנו המקום מהפקר שהזכיה בחצר בא אחר שהיה לזה פתח א' ולזה ב' פתחים וכן הוא באמת משמעות דברי המגיד משנה שממנו הוציא הב"י והרב בהג"ה דין זה א"כ קשה הא דין זה הוא ממש מ"ש המחבר ומה הוסיף הרב בהג"ה ועוד קשה דבה"ג משמע דדין זה הוא לענין אי כופין א"ע לחלוק בשיש כשיעור הזה בחצר ובסי' זה לא מיירי רק אפי' כשחולקין מדעת אם יש לו זכות יותר למי שיש לו בו פתחים וכמ"ש הסמ"ע ס"ק ב' ועוד קשה מה שסיים דאם מגיע לכ"א לפני ביתו ד"א על ד"א חולקין דמשמע דאפי' כשיש לכ"א רק פתח א' ג"כ חולקין אפי' אין בכל חלק רק ד"א על ד"א אף דליכא ד"א לכל פתח ומה שמבואר בסי' קע"א סעיף ג' דבעינן ד"א חוץ מד"א של פתחים היינו בקנו מהפקר דוקא משמע מכל הפוסקים להיפך אח"כ מצאתי בדרישה אות ג' שמניח בדברי המ"מ שממנו מוצא הדין שכצ"ל שיש לפני ביתו אויר של ח' אמות על ד"א וא"ש אך קו' הראשונות עדיין קשה לכן נראה דהג"ה זו אין מקומו כאן ומקומו לעיל בסי' קע"א סעיף ג' שכתב שצ"ל בחצר ד"א חוץ מד"א של פתחים דמשמע דאם יש לא' שני פתחים ולא' פתח א' דצריך שיהיה בחצר לכל פתח ד"א וע"ז כ' דהיינו בסתם חצירות והיינו שקנו מהפקר אבל חצר שיש לכ"א חלק ידוע דהיינו שקנו או שירשו א"צ ליתן לכ"א רק ח' אמות על ד"א אפי' לאותו שיש לו ב' פתחים ואם מקום הג"ה כאן יש חסרון דברים וכצ"ל וכן לענין כפיה לחלוק דבעינן ד"א חוץ מד"א של פתחים דוקא בסתם חצירות כו' לפני ביתו ח"א על ד"א כו' וכמו שהגיה בדרישה כצ"ל:
netivot_hamishpat_beurim.en: But a courtyard in which each has a known share. This gloss is very difficult. If it means that each party knows the specific physical portion he uses and neither uses the other's part, then even if each house has less than four cubits before it they may divide, as explained in siman 171, seif 2. If it means merely that each has a known fractional share, such as one half, or a firstborn has two shares, then that is exactly Mechaber's basic case and Rama adds nothing. Moreover, the gloss appears to address whether the parties can compel division when there is sufficient courtyard space, while this siman generally discusses how extra courtyard rights are allocated even when they divide voluntarily. The end of the gloss, saying that if each receives four by four cubits before his house they divide, is also difficult. It implies that even where each has only one entrance they may divide with only four by four, although siman 171, seif 3, requires four cubits in addition to the entrance space. Perishah already notes that Maggid Mishneh, from whom Beit Yosef and Rama derive the rule, should read that there are eight cubits by four before each house. That solves the numerical difficulty but not the earlier ones. It therefore appears that this gloss belongs in siman 171, seif 3, where Mechaber requires four cubits in the courtyard in addition to four cubits for each entrance. Rama's gloss would then mean: this applies to an ordinary courtyard whose rights arose by first use, where one person had one entrance and another two. But where each party has a known fractional ownership share through purchase or inheritance, one need not allocate four cubits for every entrance. It is enough that each receives eight by four cubits before his house, even if one has two entrances. If the gloss is retained here, missing words must be supplied to make clear that it is speaking about the coercive division rules of siman 171.

netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.he:
ואותו שהגיע לחלקו. וה"ה להיפך אם האותו שיש לו פתח א' נתן העודף דאמרי' דאלולי זה היה נותן לו עודף יותר (סמ"ע) והט"ז חולק בזה:
בכלל זה העילוי. אע"ג דעלו סתם ובלא עילוי אפילו אין הבתים שווים (סמ"ע):
בסתם חצירות. ע' הפי' בביאורים:
netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.en:
And the one to whose share it fell. The same applies in reverse: if the party who had only one entrance paid the additional amount, we assume that without this arrangement he would have had to pay an even greater premium. Sema. The Taz disagrees:
The increase is included in this. This applies even though the parties performed the division without specifying an added value, and even where the houses are not equal. Sema:
In ordinary courtyards. See the explanation in the Beurim:

rabbi_akiva_eiger.he: [שו"ע] פרץ את פצימיו. נ"ב ואם לא הי' לו כלל פצימין וסתם הפתח כתב מהרח"ש סי' י"ד דמלישנא דרש"י שכתב דלא פרץ פצימיו שלא סילק מזוזתו וכו' דגלי דעתי' שלא סילק. משמע דבעי' גילוי דעת שסופו לפותחו. הא בסתם אמרינן איבד זכותו. אבל מלישנא דהה"מ שכתב שכל שפרץ פצימיו מחשבתו ניכרת שהוא מסלק עצמו וכו' משמע דבעי' גילוי דעת שמסלק זכותו עיי"ש. ובשו"ת מהרי"ק סי' קצ"א כתב ג"כ להוכיח דהעיקר דבעינן גילוי דעת שסופו לפתחו עיי"ש:
rabbi_akiva_eiger.en: [Shulchan Aruch] He broke away its doorposts. Note: If there were no doorposts at all and he sealed the opening, Maharach Shmuel, siman 14, wrote that from Rashi's language, "he did not break away his doorposts," meaning that he did not remove his mezuzah and so forth, thereby revealing his intent not to withdraw, it follows that an affirmative indication is required that he intends ultimately to reopen it. If he simply seals it, we say that he lost his right. However, from the language of Maggid Mishneh, who wrote that whenever he breaks away the doorposts his intent is apparent that he is removing himself, it follows that an affirmative indication is required that he is relinquishing his right. See there. Responsa Maharik, siman 191, likewise wrote to prove that the primary view is that we require an indication that he intends ultimately to reopen it. See there.

turei_zahav.he: [סעיף ב' ואותו שהגיע] כו'. מ"ש הסמ"ע סק"ו ה"ה אם הבית של פתח ח' כו' לע"ד אומר אף שזהו מדברי ב"י מ"מ אינו מסתבר דק"ל א"כ כי חלקו בלא עילוי אלא שוה בשוה נמי נימא שאילולי סד"א שנוטל הב' היה צריך להוסיף יותר עכנל"ד דלא אמרי' סברא זאת שהוא בכלל העילוי אלא במקום שנותן עילוי בעל הב' פתחים דאמרינן גם זה בכלל נתינת ממונו אבל לא בכלל ניכוי החשבון לאמור שלא היה נותן לו כ"כ:
turei_zahav.en: (Seif 2: And the one to whom it fell, etc.) Sema, seif katan 6, writes that the same applies where one house has an opening eight cubits wide, etc. Although this comes from Beit Yosef, in my humble opinion it is not persuasive. If so, even where they divide without any additional payment but simply equally, we should say that had the other party known he was receiving the second property he would have demanded a larger adjustment. In my view we do not employ such reasoning by reducing the accounting. The consideration can be treated as included in the added payment only where the owner of the property with the two entrances actually pays an additional amount; then we may say that this factor too is included in the money he gives. But we cannot use it merely to reduce the calculation by saying that otherwise he would not have given as much.

turei_zahav.en: Rabbeinu wrote at the end of the siman: It appears necessary to distinguish. His meaning is as follows. He was troubled by the Rosh's statement, cited by the Beit Yosef, that the courtyard must contain six units of four by four cubits. If the Rosh speaks of a case involving loss, such as ownerless property where the owner of two entrances acquired eight cubits, it is indeed true that he cannot be compelled to divide. Since the Rosh follows the Geonim that only in ownerless property does each entrance receive four cubits, whereas this is not so in inheritance or purchase, the Rosh could not have stated that five units of four by four suffice. In ownerless property, five such units are genuinely required, since the owner of two entrances may not be deprived. The Rosh must therefore be speaking of inheritance or purchase. There, while the courtyard is jointly owned, the owner of two entrances has no advantage over the owner of one entrance. Nevertheless, one might think that he can say, “Until now we used the courtyard jointly, but if you divide, you will certainly divide equally, while I need four cubits for each entrance.” He might therefore seek to prevent division. The Rosh teaches that he is not heard, since he suffers no loss. Four cubits for one entrance, plus another four cubits in the courtyard, suffice. The same applies to ownerless property where the entrances are equal, for there too one may compel division. By contrast, where the entrances are unequal in ownerless property, division may be prevented. This explains Rabbeinu's distinction. The Rosh's case of unequal entrances concerns inheritance or purchase, where no actual loss exists. His essential point is that where division causes loss, there can be no division unless the loss is avoided. Thus, in ownerless property where one owner has two entrances and the other one entrance, he cannot be compelled to divide until there are five units of four by four cubits. One might otherwise have thought that in inheritance or purchase, since each entrance ordinarily requires four cubits, an owner with two entrances needs eight cubits for his entrances, and since the other must receive an equal amount, the whole courtyard would need six units of four by four cubits. The same thought might arise in ownerless property where the entrances are equal, because there too there is no loss. This is incorrect. Since division causes him no loss, he may be compelled once there are four cubits for one entrance and an additional four cubits in the courtyard. Rabbi Yosef Halevi speaks of this case. There is therefore no disagreement at all. Rabbeinu merely explains Rabbi Yosef Halevi and the Rosh, unlike the Beit Yosef, who raised two objections. Each objection is resolved by the other according to the explanation given here.

It does not receive four cubits. Meaning, four cubits are not assigned to its entrance as they are to the entrance of a house. The Sages gave four cubits at a house entrance for unloading one's burden, because ordinarily a donkey cannot be brought into a house to unload there. An open portico, however, can be entered with the donkey. Even if the portico itself is less than four cubits wide, we do not add courtyard space to complete four cubits, for it is no better than a house less than four cubits wide, whose entrance does not receive four cubits, as the Tur and Mechaber write below in seif 8. But if the portico stands before the entrance of a house, four cubits must be provided for the house entrance. The width of the portico itself counts toward those four cubits because the donkey can enter there. Rama therefore concludes that whatever the portico lacks from four cubits is completed from the courtyard, and the two areas together form the four cubits due to the house entrance. The Tur writes this in the name of Ri. The first part of the Mechaber follows Rashi's explanation, as the Tur cites him. See the Perishah.

meirat_einayim.en: The refuse of the courtyard, etc., but lodging troops, etc. The entire passage is the Rambam's language. In the Perishah and Derishah I demonstrated from the contrast, "but lodging troops," that in his view the term refers to the expenses of providing provisions for those lodged there. The contrast is then precise. The "refuse" at the beginning means the expense of removing refuse from the courtyard, where the residents do not wish it left and trampled into a manure heap for their fields. That expense is assessed according to entrances, because the refuse is thrown out through the entrances. The expense of feeding lodged troops, by contrast, is not assessed according to entrances but according to the people residing there. I brought several proofs that this is how the Rambam and Tur understand the matter. Others explain "lodging troops" as the refuse left behind by royal troops when they depart from their encampment. The Rif and Rosh explain that this includes not only animal manure but also earthenware jars and their lees. Such items are divided according to the number of residents. According to that explanation, the refuse at the beginning likewise means refuse that has already become a manure heap useful for fertilizing fields, and it is divided according to entrances, while the manure and jars left by troops are divided according to residents. Either way, the second clause contrasts with the first. Rama's gloss can be understood accordingly. His first explanation of "the refuse left in the courtyard" follows the second interpretation, meaning the manure heap left by the troops after their stay. His later "some say that lodging troops means what must be provided to them" refers to the expense of their food. Under that interpretation the initial refuse means the expense of removing ordinary refuse from the courtyard. Both readings maintain the contrast introduced by the word "but." This excludes the Ir Shushan's explanation, which treats the opening clause as manure for fields and the latter clause as an assessment imposed by the king, without preserving the contrast. Perhaps for that reason he omitted the word "but," but that is not correct.

netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.he: פי' הזבל שמניחין בחצר וי"א ולפי' הא' שמפרשין הזבל לענין חלוקת הזבל שמניחין בחצר מפרשין גם כן אכסניא דהיינו חלוקת הזבל שמניחין האכסנאים של מלך והי"א דמפרשי לענין ההוצאות מה שצריכין לתת להאכסנסאים של מלך מפרשים הרישא דהזבל לענין הוצאות פינוי הזבל והשתא שני הפירושים הרישא והסיפא הוה דבר והיפוכו ומדוקדק האבל שכתב המאבר (סמ"ע):
netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.en: Meaning the refuse that is left in the courtyard. According to the first interpretation, which understands "refuse" as referring to division of the refuse left in the courtyard, "royal lodgers" likewise refers to division of the refuse left by the king's guests. The second interpretation understands "royal lodgers" as referring to expenses that residents must contribute for hosting the king's guests, and accordingly understands the first clause concerning refuse as the expenses of removing refuse. Thus, under each interpretation the first and second clauses form opposite types of obligation, and the Mechaber's word "but" is precise. Sema:

אכסניא לפי בני אדם. עיין בתשו' צ"צ סימן י"ט שב' דאין הפירוש כמו שעולה על הדעת לומר דגובין מכולם בשוה אם דל ואם עשיר דהא ודאי ליתא דכיון דליכא סכנת נפשות באכסניא אין גובין אלא לפי הממון אך מה דקאמר לפי בני אדם היינו לאפוקי לפי פתחים אבל לא שיתנו כולם בשוה אלא העשיר לפי עשרו כו' וכמו שגובין ההוצאה על אכסניא לפי ממון כן מתחלקת ההכנסה מהם דהיינו הזבל וגולפא ונראה דככי דייקא לישנא דקתני לפי בני אדם ולאקאמר לפי הנפשות כו' ע"ש ועיין בתשו' שב יעקב חח"מ סי' יו"ד שביאר דבריו וכ' דהא דדחיק לפי בני אדם היינו לפי ממון זהו לפי' המפרשים הא דאכסניא היינו דגובין הוצאת אכסניא ולא ליתן חנייה בבתיהם משא"כ לפי' המפרשים דכל א' צריך ליתן חנייה דוקא ולא שיתנו שום ממון רק ותאכסנו החיל עצמם בביתו ודאי לא צריכין לדחוק כן רק הפי' לפי בני אדם היינו לפי הבעלי בתים והצ"צ גופיה מודה בהא כו' ט"ס ועמ"ש לעיל סימן קס"ג ס"ג בהגה ב' סק"ז. ועיין בתשובת במלת שבעה ח"ב סי' יו"ד בענין זה באם צריכין ליתן חנייה בבתיהם דוקא ולפעמים יש לא' שנים או שלשה בעלי מלחמות ולא' אין לו רק בע"מ א' או אין לו כלום ותובע זה שיש לו למי שאין לו שיתן לו לסיוע וכ' שפסק כפי הנראה לו פעמים בראיה ופעמים באומדנא דאם נתאכסנו אצל יהודים ע"י הפיר"ר אז נסתחפה שדהו של מי שיש לו וכן אם נתאכסנו ע"י העירונים שהיו מחלקין ביניהם ע"י פלעטין ונחנו ג"כ ליהודים ע"י פלעטין לכל א' וא' אז דיניהם דין אע"פ שלא חלקו ע"פ הערכה שיש להקהל וכ"כ בת"ה סימן שמ"ה לנידון דידיה כו' ועכשיו שנתנו העיירונים למקצת יהודים ולמקצת לא נתנו (ר"ל שלא ע"י פלעטין רק כפי רצונם) אז צריכין אותם שלא החזיקו ליתן לסיוע למי שהחזיק (לא ידענא אמאי לא רימא גם בכה"ג נסתחפה שדהו) וה"מ אם פטורים אח"כ מן העירונים אבל אם צריכים אח"כ ליתן ממון להעירונים בשביל שלא החזיקו אז פטורים מליתן לסיוע לאותן שהחזיקו. ואם יתנו העדה (העירונים) או הקוואטיר מיישטר ליהודים סך בע"מ כפי המגיע אל חנק היהודים אז יחלקו היהודים ביניהם כפי ערך הממון כו' (זהו שלא כדברי השב יעקב והצ"צ הנ"ל) ע"ש עוד והלשון מגומגם וקשה לעמוד על בירור דעתו בזה. (ובענין אם רשאי להשתדל בזה אצל הפיר"ר ע' לקמן סימן שפ"ח ס"ב בהגה ומ"ש שם) . ובתשו' כב"ח סימן קנ"ג הביאו המסגרת והעט"ז לעיל סימן קס"ג ס"ק י"ג כתב בזה וז"ל אם בעלי מלחמות הולכין מעיר לעיר ועשו אכסניא בקצת בתים ובקצת לא עשו אכסניא כולם חייבים ליתן לזה ומחשבין לפי ממון בד"א כשלקחו דרך ביזה וגזילה שלא מחק דת המלכות וכופין ליתן להם מה שביקשו מהם אבל מה שלקחו מדת המלכות דינא דמלכותא דינא וצריך להתברר איך הוא חק המלך שיגבה כן יקום עכ"ל והרב עט"צ נתב עליו ולי נראה שיש חילוק אם השמש של הקהל נתן לבעלי המלחמות אכסניא ושאר שכינים נותנין לסיוע אף שגוזלין יותר מחק שלהם פטורים מליתן הגזילה ע"ש:

pitchei_teshuva.en:
Lodging is assessed according to the people. See Tzemach Tzedek, siman 19. He explains that this does not mean that the poor and wealthy pay equal amounts. Since ordinary military billeting does not involve danger to life, the expense is assessed according to wealth. The phrase "according to the people" excludes assessment according to doorways; it means according to the householders and their means. Just as the expenses of lodging troops are apportioned according to wealth, so too any income or benefit generated by them, such as manure or discarded vessels, is apportioned on the same basis. The wording "according to the people," rather than "according to the souls," supports this understanding. Shav Yaakov, Choshen Mishpat, siman 10, explains that this interpretation applies according to those who understand the obligation as the monetary cost of military lodging. According to the view that each householder must actually provide quarters in his home rather than contribute money, "according to the people" may simply mean according to householders, and Tzemach Tzedek would agree. See what I wrote above in siman 163:3. Nachalat Shivah, part II, siman 10, discusses cases in which some Jews receive two or three soldiers while others receive one or none. He distinguishes how the soldiers were assigned. If they were billeted directly by the commanding officer, the burden falls upon the household that received them. If the municipal officials distributed quarters according to official allotments, that distribution is binding even if it does not track the community's usual tax assessment. If municipal officials assigned soldiers to some Jews arbitrarily and not pursuant to fixed allotments, those who received none must contribute to those who bore the lodging burden, provided the exempt householders are not separately required to pay the municipality for their exemption. If the officials allot a stated total number of soldiers to the Jewish community, then the Jewish householders distribute the burden among themselves according to financial assessment. His wording is difficult in places and his exact conclusion is not entirely clear. A responsum of the Bach, siman 153, cited earlier, rules that when soldiers travel from town to town and lodge in some Jewish homes but not others, all contribute according to wealth where the soldiers take by force beyond lawful governmental rules. Where the burden is imposed by valid law of the kingdom, the governing law determines the allocation. A later authority adds that if the communal shamash himself assigned quarters, the other neighbors must contribute to the legitimate burden, though they need not compensate a householder for excess amounts unlawfully extorted beyond the soldiers' entitlement.
Billeting is assessed according to the people. See Responsa Tzemach Tzedek, siman 19, who writes that this does not mean, as one might initially suppose, that the charge is collected equally from everyone, poor and rich alike. That certainly is not so, for since billeting does not involve danger to life, the charge is collected only according to wealth. Rather, the phrase "according to the people" excludes assessment according to doorways; it does not mean that all pay equally, but that the wealthy person pays according to his wealth, and so forth. Just as the expense of billeting is collected according to wealth, so too the income derived from the soldiers, namely the manure and empty casks, is divided according to wealth. It appears that the wording is precise, for the Mishnah says "according to the people" and does not say "according to the souls." See there. See also Responsa Shav Yaakov, Choshen Mishpat, siman 10, who explains his words. He writes that the Tzemach Tzedek's forced interpretation, that "according to the people" means according to wealth, is needed only according to those authorities who explain billeting as the collection of the expenses of lodging, rather than an obligation to provide lodging in one's own house. According to those who explain that each person must provide actual lodging, and no money is paid, but the soldiers themselves are quartered in his house, there is no need for that forced interpretation. "According to the people" then means according to the householders, and the Tzemach Tzedek himself agrees to this. See what I wrote above, siman 163, seif 3, second gloss, seif katan 7. See also Responsa Nachalat Shivah, part 2, siman 10, concerning whether one must provide actual lodging in his house. At times one person has two or three soldiers quartered with him, while another has only one, or none at all, and the one who has soldiers demands that the one who has none contribute toward his burden. He writes that he ruled as appeared proper to him, sometimes on the basis of proof and sometimes by assessment: if the soldiers were quartered with Jews through the official billeting authority, the loss falls upon the person to whom they were assigned. Likewise, if the townsmen distributed them among themselves by billets and assigned billets to the Jews as well, their distribution is legally effective even if they did not divide according to the community's tax assessment. Terumat HaDeshen, siman 345, likewise ruled in his case. But where the townsmen gave soldiers to some Jews and not to others, meaning not by billets but according to their own choice, then those who were not burdened must contribute to those who were. I do not know why he does not say that even in this case the loss simply fell upon the one to whom the soldiers were assigned. This applies only if those without soldiers are thereafter exempt from paying the townsmen. If they must later pay money to the townsmen because no soldiers were quartered with them, they are exempt from contributing to those who had soldiers. If the municipal body or the quartermaster assigns to the Jews a total number of soldiers corresponding to the Jewish portion, then the Jews divide that burden among themselves according to wealth. This is not consistent with the Shav Yaakov and Tzemach Tzedek cited above. See there further. His language is somewhat confused, and it is difficult to determine his precise view. Concerning whether one may exert influence with the billeting official in this matter, see below, siman 388, seif 2, in the gloss, and what I wrote there. In Responsa Bach, siman 153, cited by Misgeret HaShulchan and Atzei Levonah above, siman 163, seif katan 13, he writes: If soldiers travel from city to city and are quartered in some houses but not others, everyone must contribute to those houses, and the assessment is according to wealth. This applies when the soldiers take by plunder and robbery contrary to the law of the kingdom, and the residents are compelled to give whatever the soldiers demand. But what they take pursuant to the law of the kingdom is governed by dina d'malchuta dina, and one must determine what the king's law is; whatever that law requires stands. Atzei Levonah comments that in his view there is a distinction: if the community attendant assigned the billeting, the other neighbors must contribute, but if the soldiers themselves extort more than what the law allows, the others are exempt from contributing toward that excess. siftei_kohen.he: הזבל של חצר כו' עיין בסמ"ע ס"ק ך' עד ולא כע"ש שפי' הריש' בזבל שמזבל בו שדותיהן ואכסניא דסיפא פי' מהשהמלך מטיל על בני החצר כו' ואני אומר דיפה כוון הע"ש בזה דפי' ודבריו הם ממש דברי רש"י בש"ס דפי' זבל שבחצר אחלוקת זבל ואפ"ה פי' באכסני' שהוא להוצאות בני מלך ולהכי השמיט בע"ש תיבת אבל בכוון ויותר י"ל דאף הרמב"ם ותוס' שמפרשים דפי' אכסניא היא אהוצאת בני המלך מ"מ ס"ל דרישא דברייתא בזבל שבחצר פירושו הוא מחלוק' זבלים לזבל שדותיהן ולשון אבל שכתב הרמב"ם וטור אינו דקדוק כלל שיהיו מפרשים לדבר והפוכו וראיה לזה שכל הפוסקים המפורסמים לא הביאו פי' אחר נגד פי' רש"י בזבל שבחצר כ"א בפי' אכסניא הביאו ב' פירושים גם התוס' שמפרשים פי' אחר על אכסניא ולא כתבו פי' אחר על זבל מוכח דס"ל כפי' רש"י בזה ודוק וצ"ע לדינא בהוצאות זבלים ועיין באגודה ובחדושי אגודה:
siftei_kohen.en: The manure of the courtyard, etc. See Sema, seif katan 20, where he rejects the Levush, who explains the first clause as referring to manure used to fertilize their fields, while explaining the latter clause, concerning billeting, as the expenses imposed by the king upon the residents of the courtyard. I say that the Levush understood the matter correctly. His words are precisely those of Rashi in the Gemara, who explains 'the manure in the courtyard' as division of the manure, yet explains 'billeting' as expenses for the king's men. For this reason the Levush intentionally omitted the word 'but.' It is also possible that although the Rambam and Tosafot explain billeting as expenses for the king's men, they agree that the first clause of the baraita, concerning manure in the courtyard, means division of the manure for fertilizing their fields. The word 'but' used by the Rambam and Tur is not precise enough to prove that the two clauses must be opposites. The proof is that all the well-known authorities cite no alternative to Rashi's explanation of the manure, whereas they do cite two explanations of billeting. Tosafot likewise give another explanation of billeting without offering a different explanation of the manure, which proves that they agree with Rashi on that point. Examine this carefully. The practical law concerning the expenses of removing manure requires study. See the Agudah and Chiddushei Agudah.
